Necromancer
NEK-ro-man-ser
noun
From the Greek nekros, “a corpse, the dead,” joined to manteia, “divination”: divination by the dead. It names the darkest branch of the forbidden arts, the summoning of the departed to learn things to come.

Biblical Definition

A necromancer is one who seeks knowledge from the dead. The word is Greek — nekros, “a corpse,” joined to manteia, “divination” — and it names the darkest branch of the forbidden arts, the summoning of the departed to wring from them secrets of things to come. The law of Moses sets the necromancer last and worst in the black roll of Deuteronomy, among the abominations for which the LORD cast out the nations. Scripture gives the practice one long and terrible scene: Saul, forsaken of God, disguises himself and comes by night to the woman of Endor, saying, “I pray thee, divine unto me by the familiar spirit, and bring me him up, whom I shall name unto thee” (1Sa 28:8) — and the king who had once cut off such workers now creeps to one for a word, and hears only his own doom. Isaiah exposes the folly at its root: “when they shall say unto you, Seek unto them that have familiar spirits… should not a people seek unto their God? for the living to the dead?” (Isa 8:19). The dead do not serve the curiosity of the living; the redeemed are with their Lord, and the lost are sealed in torment. Therefore the law is flat: “Regard not them that have familiar spirits, neither seek after wizards, to be defiled by them: I am the LORD your God” (Lev 19:31).

Webster 1828 Definition

One who professes to foretell future events by communication with the dead — a diviner by corpses.

expand to see more

NECROMANCER, one who pretends to foretell future events by holding converse with the dead; a conjurer.

From Greek nekros, “the dead,” and manteia, “divination.”

It is the last and gravest name in the forbidden roll of the law.

Saul sought a word from the dead through the woman of Endor, and heard his doom (1Sa 28:8).

Isaiah asks why a people should seek the dead for the living rather than their God (Isa 8:19).

Key Scripture

1Sa 28:8 — "And Saul disguised himself, and put on other raiment, and he went, and two men with him, and they came to the woman by night: and he said, I pray thee, divine unto me by the familiar spirit, and bring me him up, whom I shall name unto thee."

Isa 8:19 — "And when they shall say unto you, Seek unto them that have familiar spirits, and unto wizards that peep, and that mutter: should not a people seek unto their God? for the living to the dead?"

Lev 19:31 — "Regard not them that have familiar spirits, neither seek after wizards, to be defiled by them: I am the LORD your God."

Lev 20:6 — "And the soul that turneth after such as have familiar spirits, and after wizards, to go a whoring after them, I will even set my face against that soul, and will cut him off from among his people."

Modern Corruption

Necromancy lives on as the seance, the “medium” and psychic who claim to contact the departed, and the grief-industry that promises a word from the dead — the same sin the law names an abomination.

expand to see more

This is a living, thriving corruption. The seance never closed; it moved to television and the internet. The celebrity “medium” who claims to relay messages from a deceased mother, the app that offers to “connect” the grieving with the dead, the paranormal show that summons spirits for entertainment — all of it is necromancy, divination by the dead, however tender its marketing. It preys on grief with a counterfeit comfort, and it teaches the mourner to seek the living among the dead. Scripture treats it not as harmless closure but as the gravest of the forbidden arts, an abomination that provoked the LORD to empty whole nations from their land.

The Bible’s answer is both a warning and a hope. The warning is Saul: the man who dabbled in the dead died for it, and enquired not of the LORD (compare 1Ch 10:13). The hope is that the dead in Christ are not lost to a medium’s summons but safe in the hand of God, awaiting a resurrection no seance could purchase. Isaiah presses the question that ends the matter: “should not a people seek unto their God? for the living to the dead?” (Isa 8:19). What answers the necromancer is never the beloved departed; it is a lying spirit wearing a loved one’s voice. The Christian brings his grief to the throne of grace, not to the tomb, and waits for the trumpet.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

The word is nekros (the dead) + manteia (divination) — one who consults the dead for knowledge.

expand to see more

Necromancer — from Greek nekros, “the dead,” and manteia, “divination.”

It names the darkest of the arts forbidden in the law of Moses.

Saul’s night at Endor is Scripture’s great scene of necromancy (1Sa 28:8).

Isaiah rebukes seeking the dead when a people might seek their God (Isa 8:19).

The LORD sets His face against the soul that turns after such workers (Lev 20:6).

Usage

"A necromancer consults the dead — Saul’s midnight errand to Endor is the AV’s one long scene of it."

"The word joins nekros, the dead, to manteia, divination: the gravest of the condemned arts."

"The modern seance and celebrity medium are necromancy in a studio — the law calls it an abomination still."
